title: Rain Caught Between Bars
statement:
You get an array heights describing a row of bars, each 1 unit wide, standing side by side. Bar i is heights[i] units tall.

Rain falls on the whole row. Water stays wherever it is walled in on both sides; anything that can flow off the left or right edge is lost. Return the total number of units of water left standing.

examples.why: Between the 3 and the 4 the level is 3: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 units. Between the 4 and the 2 the level is 2: 2 more units.
A single hill. Water on either slope runs off the edge.
The tall 5 does not set the level: water would spill over the 3 on the right. The level is 3, holding 2 + 1 + 2.

hints: Think about one position at a time. How high can the water above bar i rise?
The level above i is min(tallest bar on its left, tallest bar on its right), and the water there is that level minus heights[i], if positive. Can you get both maxima without rescanning?

Two pointers from the ends, each tracking the tallest bar it has passed. Whichever side has the lower running maximum is the side whose level is already known, so settle that position and move that pointer.

explain.intuition:
Look at one position. Water above it rises until it would spill over the lower of two walls: the tallest bar somewhere to its left and the tallest bar somewhere to its right. So the water there is min(leftMax, rightMax) − heights[i]. Precomputing both maxima as arrays already gives an O(n) answer.

Two pointers drop the arrays. Keep leftMax for everything the left pointer has passed and rightMax for the right pointer. If leftMax < rightMax, the left position's true right maximum is at least rightMax, which is bigger than leftMax. So the shorter side, leftMax, already decides its level, and you can settle it without knowing anything else. The same holds mirrored for the right side.
steps: If the left bar is lower: update leftMax with heights[lo], add leftMax − heights[lo] to total, and move lo right.
Otherwise do the same on the right side with rightMax and move hi left.
pitfalls: Using the tallest bar on one side only. In [5, 1, 2, 1, 3] the 5 is not the level; the 3 on the other side is.
Filling between the first and last bar to the height of the second tallest bar overall. Several separate pools can have different levels, like in the first example.
Updating the running maximum after adding water instead of before. The bar itself may be the new maximum, and then it holds 0, never a negative amount.

solutions.title: Scan both sides for every position
solutions.idea: For each position, walk left and right to find the tallest bars, then add the water above it.

solutions.title: Prefix and suffix maxima
solutions.idea: Precompute the tallest bar up to each position from the left and from the right. The water at i is the smaller of the two minus heights[i].

solutions.title: Two pointers with running maxima
solutions.idea: Settle the side whose running maximum is lower: its level is already decided, whatever lies in the middle.

followups: Solve it with a stack that fills one horizontal layer at a time. When is that version more natural?
The bars form a 2D grid of heights and water can escape off any edge. What changes? (Hint: a heap.)
